title: Not Ansible: Puppet, Chef, and Salt
intro: The Server Fleet Ops category used Ansible, which pushes changes over SSH when you run it. The older generation of configuration management works the other way: an agent on every server pulls its configuration from a central server on a schedule and corrects any drift. Many large, long-lived fleets still run on Puppet, Chef, or Salt. You're on a server managed by Puppet.

steps.prompt: See what Puppet would change on this server right now, without changing anything.
steps.fake_output:
Info: Applying configuration version '1790950000'
Notice: /Stage[main]/Nginx/File[/etc/nginx/nginx.conf]/content:
--- /etc/nginx/nginx.conf
+++ /tmp/puppet-file20261002
-worker_connections 8192;
+worker_connections 768;
Notice: /Stage[main]/Nginx/File[/etc/nginx/nginx.conf]/content: current_value '{sha256}9f1c...', should be '{sha256}41bb...' (noop)
Notice: Applied catalog in 4.12 seconds
steps.explanation: Puppet would put worker_connections back to 768: someone edited the file by hand to 8192.
steps.why: --noop is Ansible's --check: a dry run with a diff. It has just shown the defining behaviour of pull-based tools: the hand edit is drift, and the agent will revert it at its next run, by default every 30 minutes. Fixes made directly on a Puppet-managed server quietly undo themselves, which confuses everyone who hasn't seen it before. The change has to go into the Puppet code.

steps.prompt: Find out which Puppet server this agent takes its configuration from.
steps.why: The agent sends facts about the machine to the server, which compiles a catalog, the complete desired state for that node, and sends it back. That central server is a dependency of the whole fleet's configuration, and the agents authenticate to it with certificates, which need signing when a new server joins.

steps.prompt: You've edited a manifest, modules/nginx/manifests/init.pp. Check its syntax before committing.
steps.why: Puppet's language is declarative: resources such as file, package, and service, with their desired state, and Puppet works out the order from the dependencies between them. That's a different mental model from an Ansible playbook, which runs top to bottom. Validation and linting belong in CI, with changes tested on a canary group of nodes before the whole fleet.

steps.prompt:
Chef works the same way with different words: cookbooks and recipes, written in Ruby, and a chef-client agent. On a Chef-managed node, what does 'sudo chef-client --why-run' do?
  a) Applies everything immediately
  b) A dry run: shows what the client would change, without changing it
  c) Uninstalls Chef
  d) Uploads the cookbook
Type the letter.
steps.fake_output:
Puppet : puppet agent --test --noop
Chef   : chef-client --why-run
Salt   : salt '<target>' state.apply test=True
Ansible: ansible-playbook --check --diff
steps.hint: Every tool in this family has a 'tell me, don't do it' mode.
steps.why: Learn each tool's dry-run flag first; it's what makes an unfamiliar system safe to explore. 'knife node list' and 'knife node show' are Chef's way to see the fleet from the server's side.

steps.prompt: Salt keeps a persistent connection from each minion to the master, so it can also run commands across the fleet instantly. On the Salt master, check which minions respond.
steps.fake_output:
web-1:
    True
web-2:
    True
db-1:
    True
web-3:
    Minion did not return. [No response]
steps.why: Salt combines state management with fast remote execution: the same targeting works for 'apply this state' and 'run this command now'. That power cuts both ways: the master can run anything as root on every minion, so its compromise is the fleet's. A minion that doesn't return is either down or has lost its connection, and is silently missing every change until someone notices.
